newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian team starts work on economic masterplan.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian team starts work on economic masterplan.

text.p: Nigeria started work on Tuesday on a blueprint for economic development into the next century.
A committee set up by military ruler General Sani Abacha met in the capital Abuja to open discussions on a strategic plan for Africa's most populous nation, to be delivered by September 1997.
The committee's 172 members include traditional rulers, newspaper editors, prominent bankers, businessmen and the local chief executives of major multinational oil firms.

"Our objective in this two-day workshop is essentially to brainstorm on our assignment to enable us to break into the methodology and process we shall be adopting as from the next workshop in January," said committee chairman Ernest Shonekan.
A former head of state Shonekan, who is a keen advocate of economic deregulation, was overthrown by Abacha in 1993.
Abacha launched "Vision 2010", which is modelled on plans in other countries such as Malaysia, at an economic conference in Abuja in September.

Shonekan said the methodology being used by the committee had been developed by Shell, the largest of the multinational oil companies pumping the crude oil on which Nigeria is almost totally reliant for foreign earnings.
"We should not be unduly burdened about borrowing ideas for use in developing this nation. Whatever tool or methodology we borrow we shall get the Nigerian solution," Shonekan said.
When Abacha unveiled the plan he said it aimed to raise Nigeria's gross domestic product through agriculture and industrialisation as well as to improve literacy levels, healthcare and employment.
Abacha's tight fiscal policies have led to a drop in annual inflation from above 70 percent in 1995 after a four-fold increase in fuel prices to less than 30 percent.
But there are still few signs of economic growth or any increase in consumer spending.
Although among the 10 leading producers of crude oil in the world, Nigeria is among the poorest nations on the basis of per capita income, due mainly to corruption and political instability.
Africa's most populous nation of 100 million plunged into turmoil in June 1993 when the army annulled an election that would have restored democracy.
Alleged human right abuses culminating in last year's hanging of nine minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa turned Nigeria into an international pariah.
Abacha has promised to hand over to a democratically-elected president in 1998.
But his critics suspect that he may intend to continue in power through elections and point to "Vision 2010" as an indication that he does not intend to leave office quickly.

"A long term economic plan is a good idea as long as it is not just an excuse for keeping the military in power and prolonging the political crisis," said one member of the opposition National Democratic Coalition.
Numerous grand economic plans in the past have borne little fruit and sceptics say this one will have nothing new to add.

"I want to appeal to the many cynics to be a little more patient with us. We too are frustrated. Since we have no other place to go than Nigeria we shall not give up our efforts to search for solutions," said Shonekan.
